items.title: South Africa have pushed the limits of rugby – time to show they still have the edge
items.summary:
Rassie Erasmus has forged an iron bond in his squad but France could push them to breaking point at Twickenham

At its best, Test rugby is a game played right out on the edge, where the players push the very limits of what anyone ought to be capable of. Out there the sport sells itself. In those moments it doesn’t matter if you know what a 50-22 is, or whether that was a hip-drop tackle or not, and no one needs a new Hemisphere Shield, or another message on the big screen telling everyone in the stadium to “Make Some Noise!” When it reaches that pitch of incomparable intensity, emotion and endeavour, Test rugby demands your attention whether you know it all or nothing at all.

Stretches of this Nations Championship have been played out there, on the farthest reaches of the sport. Wales lived there for 80 minutes in their 35-28 win over the All Blacks a fortnight ago and were rewarded with one of the most famous results in their history. England came closer to it than they had been in a very long time during their own record 37-12 victory against New Zealand a week later. France got there when they were clinging on to their two-point win against South Africa in Paris, so did Ireland in the closing moments in Dublin…
items.t: South Africa have pushed the limits of rugby – time to show they still have the edge

items.title: Basque to the future: Andoni Iraola fired up for first Merseyside derby

Liverpool head coach sees parallels with Athletic v Sociedad derby as he comes up against his old foe David Moyes

“I haven’t lived this derby,” Andoni Iraola acknowledged, and yet he already feels it. A former Athletic Bilbao captain coming up against an ex-Real Sociedad head coach needs no instruction on the importance of winning a derby, whether in the Basque country or on Merseyside. But this week, as the Liverpool head coach approaches his first experience of the latter, there has been no escape.

“It has been very easy for me here,” says Iraola of his five months on Merseyside. “Family-wise we have settled in really well. People here are very friendly, they love to talk to you but in a very respectful way. This week there has been a lot [of interaction with Liverpool fans], especially with playing big games against United and Everton. ‘We need to win, we need to win,’ they say.”

items.title: Brit-splaining Botham and the impossible task of defining a sporting life without limits | Will Woodward
items.summary:
Explaining the England all-rounder and now great-grandfather reveals a career that refuses to fit in a single box

Across the Guardian sportsdesk this week it emerged that a young American colleague didn’t know who Ian Botham was. And why should she? She is young and American. And so the rest of us Brit-splained in five sentences, rehearsed here – and edited to make us sound better than we actually did.

Botham is comfortably among the top five most famous living British sportspeople, certainly among those of a certain age. In 1981 he won (almost) single‑handed (arguably) the greatest Ashes series by bending it to his will. He was on the front pages as well as back in the 1980s, for soft drugs, suspensions and shagging. He is a member of the House of Lords. He is the most English of sports stars, Australians love him, and his grandson James plays rugby union for Wales, which is why we started talking about him.

items.t: Brit-splaining Botham and the impossible task of defining a sporting life without limits | Will Woodward

items.title: Why have things started to go wrong for Manchester City under Enzo Maresca?
items.summary:
A sensational start for the Italian was swiftly followed by a dismal run and long faces in the team

This is the great known unknown in Manchester City’s run of one win – in addition to victory on penalties against Brighton in the Carabao Cup – in seven matches. After guilty verdicts were returned regarding the breaking of Premier League financial rules, Enzo Maresca’s team went to Anfield and handed Liverpool a 3-0 schooling. Yet this proved the falsest of dawns, with Andoni Iraola’s nascent side perhaps caught in a bad moment. City have since managed one league victory (3-2 over Ipswich, six days later) and two more wins in regulation time (in the Champions League) in 10 matches. The sequence includes one point from the past four league fixtures. Maresca argues that his, too, is an embryonic project so there will be uneven form. “I am not a magician,” he said on Friday. But it is also fair to ponder whether, after the adrenaline surge of an us-against-the-world mentality carried City to the Liverpool and Ipswich wins, the grim reality of what the guilty verdict may mean for careers is affecting players. City have appealed against the ruling, saying they are “innocent of the accusations”.
items.t: Why have things started to go wrong for Manchester City under Enzo Maresca?

items.title: Nigel Starmer-Smith obituary
items.summary:
England rugby union player who became one of the best-loved commentators in the game over a 42-year broadcasting career

Nigel Starmer-Smith was an England rugby scrum-half whose international debut at Twickenham, five days before his 25th birthday on Christmas Day in 1969, was a historic first ever win for England over South Africa. But it was as a broadcaster that he was best known. After his playing career ended he became a schoolteacher, then made a move to the BBC where in the 1980s he fronted Rugby Special, a Sunday TV highlights programme, which gave the then-amateur sport of rugby union a wide national audience.

The undisputed voice of rugby was the lilting Scottish brogue of Bill McLaren, but Starmer-Smith, who has died aged 81, became the voice of the English shires. In his clipped, professional tones, he would tell his post-prandial Sunday audience the news from the muddy touchlines of places then familiar on the English rugby map: Bedford, Coventry, Otley, Redruth. Change was in the air, but rugby union was some years from its professional revolution in 1995 and, in England at least, Starmer-Smith represented a now lost cosy world of mud, fellowship and beer.

items.t: Nigel Starmer-Smith obituary

items.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
items.summary:
Liam Delap can exploit Chelsea’s defensive woes while Senne Lammens is under pressure against Brentford

Nottingham Forest’s last couple of seasons have been a story of good runs and bad runs, but it may help to know that last season’s encounters with Chelsea both presaged changes of fortune. After they lost to Chelsea in October, a seventh defeat in 10 winless games, Forest’s form improved and they won seven of their next 12 in all competitions. But after beating Chelsea in May, their seventh victory in a 10-game unbeaten run, Forest’s form dipped dramatically and they have won only twice since. Oliver Glasner’s criticism of players whose “standards [are] not high enough” is clearly designed to raise them. Time will tell if it has worked but the key man this week is one who should have no issues with motivation and whose English is at least decent. Liam Delap, facing the side that signed and swiftly discarded him, could really trouble Wesley Fofana and Levi Colwill. The Chelsea centre-back pairing were described as playing like “two novices” by Jamie Carragher after they were outfought by Dominic Calvert-Lewin last week. “Until they sign that dominant centre-back and leader, they’ve got absolutely no chance of achieving anything,” Carragher concluded. items.title: Éric Cantona: ‘If I regret something about the kung fu kick, it’s that I would love to kick him in another place’
items.summary:
Before the release of a new documentary, the unrepentant Manchester United icon reflects on his deep bond with English football and his darker instincts

“I’m an angel and a demon,” Éric Cantona says intently during a gripping new documentary about his life on and off the football pitch. “And an angel or a demon, you love him or you hate him. I’m far from being the person with the greatest integrity. I’m far from being the person who always tells the truth. I’m far from being the person who has never been hypocritical. Maybe I’m a good person, but I can also be a flower of evil. It’s the first time in my life I’ve realised this. I am a flower of evil, and I find it very beautiful.”

It’s hard to know what to expect from the only written interview pinned to the release of Cantona: Flower of Evil. Joel Cantona has warned that his famous brother will walk out at any mention of the enduring crisis surrounding Manchester United, whether it’s a question about Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival or the Glazer family’s ruinous ownership of the club.

items.title: Banton’s ascent to England leadership role vindicates all-in approach to white-ball game
items.summary:
Batter assumes vice-captaincy and is set to step in as skipper in Canberra, with appointment a potential pointer to side’s future limited-overs direction


When Will Jacks broke his hand at the MCG last Saturday night – his birthday ruined and his tour of Australia over – there were a few directions England could have turned as regards the vice-captaincy. Plenty of teams happily do without an official deputy, of course. But with Harry Brook jetting off to join the Test tour of South Africa after the fourth of these five T20 internationals, a replacement will be required when the series wraps up in Canberra.

Phil Salt was one option. For all of his unfettered aggression, powered by those tattooed, Popeye-like forearms, the opener is an intelligent, thoughtful cricketer very much in tune with the rhythms of T20. As well as two seasons captaining in the Hundred, most recently with Welsh Fire, Salt previously deputised for Jos Buttler against Australia at home two years ago.
